entries.title: Google's Gemini agents claim the first proven L[1/3] algorithm for factoring any whole number
entries.who: Google Research and Google DeepMind (Cogentic team)
entries.system: Cogentic, an agent framework running on Gemini 4
entries.sum: Google posted six papers on November 25 that it says its Cogentic agents wrote from a single prompt. The lead one claims a randomized algorithm that factors every integer in time L[1/3, 105] with no unproven assumptions, matching the exponent of the number field sieve, which only reaches L[1/3] heuristically; the best proven bound since 1992 had been L[1/2, 1]. Companion papers claim a deterministic factoring method in time L[3/4] and faster provable discrete logarithms in finite fields of small characteristic.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed and not independently checked. Google says Lean 4 proofs exist but has not released them. The constant 105 is far larger than the number field sieve's roughly 1.9, so this is a theory result that does nothing to speed up attacks on real encryption keys.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4, ruling out the hoped-for 2
entries.sum: A paper posted on November 24 claims a matching lower bound for multiplying two n by n matrices: any formal arithmetic circuit needs at least half of n to the power 9/4 multiplications or divisions, over every field. Together with the 9/4 upper bound OpenAI's model claimed earlier, which others have since extended to every field, that would fix the exponent at exactly 9/4 and refute the long-held conjecture that it could be pushed down to 2. A companion paper with the same tensor-geometry method claims to prove the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture with a base depending only on the number of petals.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and OpenAI is the only source. The Lean formalization covers division-free circuits only, not the full statement with division, and OpenAI says results in its repository that lack full formal proofs could have issues. No outside expert has commented on the lower bound yet.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims an answer to Smale's ninth problem and disproves the polynomial Hirsch conjecture
entries.sum: In the same November 24 batch, one paper claims a deterministic algorithm that solves any linear program with real coefficients in a number of steps polynomial in just the numbers of variables and constraints, a question Steve Smale made the ninth on his list of problems. A second paper claims simple polytopes with n facets whose graphs have diameter growing faster than any power of n, disproving the polynomial Hirsch conjecture; Santos's earlier counterexample, a 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets, broke only Hirsch's original bound of n minus d steps.
entries.open: Neither paper is peer reviewed and no independent expert has checked them; OpenAI is the only source. The Lean proof of the linear programming result covers rational inputs only, not arbitrary real coefficients. The Hirsch result has a Lean formalization of its main statements.

entries.title: Anthropic and OpenAI each post AI-found proofs that VP and VNP are different
entries.system: Internal research Claude model; OpenAI models (unnamed)
entries.sum: On November 23 both companies released papers claiming to settle Leslie Valiant's 1979 conjecture that the permanent of a matrix cannot be computed by polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, the algebraic counterpart of P versus NP, over every field. Anthropic's 70-page paper, credited to Claude, proves that such circuits need more than m to the power c·(log m)^(1/3) gates and comes with a Lean 4 formalization; OpenAI's 30-page paper gives a bound of the form exp(Ω((log n)^(5/4))) and links a Lean proof of the class separation. Neither result says anything about P versus NP for ordinary Boolean circuits.
entries.open: Neither paper is peer reviewed. Anthropic says no human mathematician has checked its proof, and that only AI readers judged whether its Lean statement file says what is meant; an outside rebuild of the Lean code on November 24 passed every mechanical check but cannot settle that question either. One consequence in Anthropic's paper, on determinantal complexity, is not formalized. On November 24 OpenAI replaced its paper with two companion preprints: one claims circuits for the permanent need more than exp(c(log N)^2/(log log N)^2) gates outside characteristic two, the other an explicit grid polynomial that separates the whole chain of classes VF, VBP, VP and VNP, which its Lean code proves for exact circuits over every field. No outside mathematician has assessed either set of claims.

entries.title: MiniMax says its in-house AI found attacks on eight experimental cryptographic designs
entries.who: MiniMax Cyber Team (Lili Tang, Hao Jiang, Yansong Feng; led by Tianyi Li and Guancheng Li)
entries.sum: On November 20 the Chinese AI company MiniMax published papers and code for attacks that it says were mainly discovered by an unreleased internal model, against eight research-grade ciphers, hash functions and post-quantum schemes. They include 94 private keys recovered in the TII McEliece challenges, 55 of them never solved before, with speedups of up to 43,400 times; recovery of a HAWK-256 signing key in about 31 minutes; a forgery against the CAESAR-winning COLM cipher using two queries; and collisions in the Blender and Waterfall hash functions found in under a second.
entries.open: MiniMax is the only source, nothing has been peer reviewed, and the company does not say how much of the work people did. None of the targets is a deployed standard such as AES, RSA or SHA-256; most are challenge sets, reduced-round versions or older competition candidates.

entries.title: OpenAI says its general-purpose models designed proteins that bound their targets in the lab
entries.who: OpenAI, with wet-lab work by its research partner Onava
entries.system: GPT-6.2 and an unreleased internal OpenAI model
entries.sum: OpenAI reported on November 24 that its GPT-6 models designed protein shapes and sequences by reasoning and writing code, without calling a specialist biology model to make the designs, and that the proteins were then built and tested in a laboratory. Of 322 small binder designs aimed at five human proteins, 35 bound their intended target, a hit rate of about 11 percent, with 18 of the hits against IL-17A. Redesigned antibody loops did better: 128 of 182 designs against IL-4Ra showed binding, about 70 percent, and 179 of 272 redesigned fragments of five therapeutic antibodies still bound their original target.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and OpenAI is the only source; the lab testing was done by a partner company, Onava. The models are not public and one of the two is internal, so nobody outside can repeat the designs. Binding in a dish is a long way from a drug, and the report says the models were still clearly worse than a specialist tool at predicting a whole protein's structure from its sequence. Specialist models also supplied sequences for some designs and helped choose which ones to test.

entries.title: Mathematicians using Claude and Codex claim Navier–Stokes fluids can blow up with no outside force
entries.who: Levent Alpöge (Anthropic) and Tristan Buckmaster (New York University); the Euler paper adds Matei Coiculescu (NYU)
entries.sum: A 79-page paper posted on November 20 claims smooth starting data for the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations whose solution breaks down in finite time with no external force, the version of the Millennium Prize problem that OpenAI's forced result in September did not reach. The authors say Anthropic's models wrote the first force-free proof from their earlier drafts and that they then reworked it with Claude and Codex; it comes with a Lean formalization of about 600,000 lines in roughly 2,270 files. A companion 55-page paper with Coiculescu, also done with heavy AI help, builds smooth periodic data for the 3D Euler equations whose vorticity becomes infinite in finite time.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and no outside expert has checked it. The numerical certificate the proof depends on has not been released, only its hash, and the 128-bit interval-arithmetic check sits outside the Lean code. The Lean files were patched on release day and the patched package was not rebuilt. Buckmaster calls the write-up unpolished; Terence Tao says it is technically readable and its strategy is clear, but a proper written proof still needs work.

entries.title: Complexity theorist proves NL = UL, saying GPT-6.2 Astra found the proof
entries.sum: A short paper posted on November 20 shows that any problem a nondeterministic machine can solve with logarithmic memory can also be solved with the same memory by a machine that has at most one accepting path, settling a long-standing conjecture in complexity theory. The key step is a simple, memory-efficient way to assign weights to the points of a layered graph so that the lightest route between any two connected points is unique; earlier unconditional results needed noticeably more memory, such as log to the power 3/2. In a disclosure at the end of the paper, Hoza says he used GPT-6.2 Astra to discover the proof and to help prepare the paper, and that he takes responsibility for every claim.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and the paper does not say which steps came from the model. On November 22 the open-source cslib-frontier project merged a Lean formalization of the main theorem that passed its automated checks and two reviewers, but a separate check of the paper's central weight generator was not merged. The result does not settle whether NL equals L, or P versus NP.

entries.title: Gemini agents prove a weaker form of the 1995 sample compression conjecture
entries.who: Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Shay Moran, Grigoris Velegkas, Di Wang and Manfred K. Warmuth, with Google
entries.system: Cogentic multi-agent orchestration running on Gemini 4 Carbon
entries.sum: A preprint posted on November 18 shows that any yes-or-no concept class of VC dimension d can be compressed to about d squared times log squared d labelled examples, settling the polynomial version of a learning-theory conjecture posed by Floyd and Warmuth in 1995. The best general bound before this, from Moran and Yehudayoff in 2016, grew exponentially with d. The authors say an agent system on Gemini 4 Carbon found the proof on its own, stepping down from a d to the 16th bound to the final one, at a cost of about $344 in API fees; the people simplified and wrote it up.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and the authors, who include Google researchers, are the only source. The original conjecture, a scheme of size proportional to d, is still open.

entries.title: Gemini agents design cheaper quantum algorithms and prove them correct in Lean
entries.who: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI
entries.system: Teams of Gemini 4 agents working in the Lean theorem prover
entries.sum: Agent teams wrote quantum programs against specifications that people stated in Lean, and Lean checked both that each program is correct and what it costs. The headline result is a routine for preparing an arcsin state whose estimated cost, measured as logical qubits times T gates, is about 290 times lower than a published design. The agents also cut estimated costs about 12-fold for a fusion stopping-power simulation, about 8-fold for a photochemistry simulation and about 2.5-fold for a drug-metabolism enzyme, and found up to 2.57 times fewer rounds for a multi-target Grover search.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and Google is the only source. Every figure is a resource estimate on paper, not a run on quantum hardware, and some baselines were adjusted by the authors. The circuits are still far beyond what the first error-corrected machines are expected to run. On November 23 DeepMind published the work on its blog and released the Lean library, the problem specifications and the verified solutions on GitHub, so the proofs can now be rebuilt by anyone.

entries.title: OpenAI says its models redesigned parts of its own AI chip and found gains in AMD processor designs
entries.sum: OpenAI says changes its models proposed for Jalapeño, its first in-house inference chip, shrank the logic area of the vector unit by about 13% and the matrix unit by about 10%, and that these changes worked in the finished silicon. One redesigned multiplier used about 15% less area and finished in one clock cycle instead of two. On AMD's flagship GPU designs the models found power, performance and area gains of up to 14% over heavily tuned baselines, and some of those changes are in a chip AMD has sent for manufacturing.
entries.open: OpenAI is the only source, and AMD is not quoted. The baselines are not disclosed, the Jalapeño area figures come from synthesis rather than final layout, and no test results have been reported for the AMD chip.

entries.title: Mathematician says he and Claude have proved the Riemann hypothesis, and posts only Lean code
entries.sum: In a four-page note posted on November 20, Levent Alpöge says that, working with Claude, he found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are spread out, and that the method also settles the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He has released only a Lean formalization, split into 14 archive files; a footnote saying an AI-written English version ran past 250,000 pages was, he later said, a joke. He credits Claude with key steps near the end, including the idea of chaining theta lifts about the square root of X times.
entries.open: The Lean check is now strong: the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement saying they are fully confident the proof is correct, and several people have rebuilt it independently. On November 21 Michael Rubinstein of the University of Waterloo reported that all 175,187 modules compile and pass Lean's kernel and rest only on Lean's three standard axioms. On November 25 Luke Sernau posted two much shorter Lean editions of the same five theorems, about 300,000 and 76,000 lines; MIT's Andrew Sutherland reports that both build cleanly, use only the standard axioms and pass several independent checkers, though the strictest comparison of the longer edition had not finished. Readable mathematics is still thin: Rubinstein's AI-assisted guide breaks the zeta case into thirteen hypotheses it does not prove, and no mathematician has reviewed the argument itself. There is no paper from Alpöge and no peer review. Alpöge has said the 250,000-page figure was a joke and conceded his Lean code contains much unneeded material. The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the problem as active but not solved, since its rules require publication and two years of scrutiny, and Kevin Buzzard says nobody yet understands what the proof shows. A separate, all-human draft proof by Alessandro Masullo, posted by Ravi Vakil the same day, has drawn objections and is not accepted.

entries.title: Claude agents settle two open problems in black hole physics
entries.who: Anthropic (project set up by researcher Hongbin Chen)
entries.sum: Anthropic says Claude agents finished a calculation set up in 2003 but never completed, showing that a transition in a simplified model universe is abrupt, as Hawking and Page predicted for black holes. A second result raises a long-standing bound in the modular bootstrap from about 8.5 to about 9.13, which Anthropic says is the best possible. Independent agents redid nearly every step, a physicist checked the main results, and Anthropic says the bootstrap result was verified in Lean.
entries.open: Anthropic is the main source. Both preprints are unreviewed, list no human authors and are labelled primarily AI-generated. Anthropic says neither result describes our universe or has practical use.

entries.title: GPT-6 Astra credited with the proof behind a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model
entries.who: Nathaniel Craig (UC Santa Barbara, visiting scientist at OpenAI)
entries.sum: Putting the Standard Model on a spacetime grid has been stuck for decades because the weak force treats left- and right-handed particles differently, and Lüscher's fix for simpler theories had not been carried over to the full model in more than 25 years. Craig says he had a strategy but could not prove it in every case, and that Astra turned it into a construction and led the detailed proof. The preprint, posted October 6, builds a gauge-invariant fermion measure on four-dimensional lattices for a class of theories that includes the Standard Model, and comes with a Lean 4 formalization.
entries.open: The model's role rests on Craig's own account, published on OpenAI's science blog. Three lattice theorists read the work privately, but no outside assessment has been published. Reflection positivity and a link to a continuum theory are not established, and Craig calls it an answer in principle more than in practice.

entries.title: Gemini agents help prove the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, with a batch of new algorithm results
entries.who: Google Research with CUHK and other academic co-authors
entries.sum: The 2013 conjecture says no one-bit summary of a noisy signal carries more information than simply reading off a single input bit. Google says Gemini found counterexamples to a broader version, worked out most of the analytical bounds and interval-arithmetic certificates, and extended the proof from balanced to unbalanced functions without human input; the whole proof is formalized in about 50 million lines of Lean 4. The same post lists about ten further new results, including a deterministic Boolean matrix multiplication algorithm that answers an open question from STOC 2024 and the first n-bit functions needing more than n/2 quantum queries.
entries.open: Google and its co-authors are the only source, and nothing here has been peer reviewed or independently reproduced. People supplied key steps: the CUHK team proposed the function that cut the problem to a 14-variable optimization and gave one analytical bound. Google gives no count of problems attempted or failed.

entries.title: AI system proves the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture on the limits of quantum speedups
entries.system: PSI research system running a non-public Anthropic model
entries.sum: The conjecture, open since 2008, says every bounded low-degree polynomial has at least one input bit with sizeable influence. PSI's system had a full proof by day three of its run and then tightened the bound twice, ending at an influence of at least about 0.0025·v^(5/2)/d^6 for variance v and degree d, where earlier bounds shrank exponentially with the degree. It follows that a quantum algorithm cannot save exponentially many input reads on typical random inputs to a yes/no problem.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and the model is not public. David Turturean posted the proof on arXiv on November 6, and four computer scientists led by Guy Blanc posted a reworked exposition on November 8; they say they worked to understand it, which is not a formal independent check. The result limits input reads, not total running time.

entries.title: Deep learning finds an ECG signal that flags sudden cardiac death risk
entries.sum: A model trained on Swedish heart tracings linked to death records picked out a pattern in ordinary ECGs that marks people at high risk of sudden cardiac death. The group it flagged died suddenly at about 7% a year, against 4.6% for the group picked by the standard pumping-strength test, and the pattern held in patient records from the US and Taiwan.
entries.open: Nobody yet knows what the signal is biologically, and it is not in clinical use.

entries.title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts what a DNA variant does in one chosen cell type
entries.sum: The model takes a stretch of DNA plus a tissue or cell state and predicts gene activity there. It recovered a known inflammatory bowel disease mechanism in gut macrophages and predicted that a variant tied to severe COVID-19 disrupts gene activity most in activated T cells.
entries.open: The findings are computational predictions that still need lab confirmation, and the announcement names no journal.

entries.title: AI agents formally verify the code behind Signal's encryption
entries.system: AlphaProof Code, agents on Gemini 4 Carbon
entries.sum: In about four weeks, agents wrote millions of lines of machine-checked Lean proof showing that the compiled Signal protocol code keeps its core security promises. When researchers put two old, already-fixed bugs back into a copy of the code, the system proved each buggy version insecure.
entries.open: A proof is only as good as its specification. Those were written and reviewed by people but have not had an outside audit, and no previously unknown bugs were reported.

entries.title: AI agents find two new weaknesses in retired RSA-1024 encryption
entries.who: Google DeepMind with UC San Diego and Inria
entries.sum: The agents found a signature-forgery shortcut that is up to 1,600 times faster on paper when an attacker controls only a small part of the signed data, and a batch method that cuts the cost of factoring each additional key about 30-fold.
entries.open: Both headline figures are theoretical or asymptotic, not measured attacks. Keys of 2048 bits and larger are unaffected.

entries.title: Proteins designed from plain-language descriptions work in the lab
entries.sum: Pinal turns a written description of a desired function into protein sequences. It produced working proteins on all four test tasks, a plastic-degrading enzyme among them, and one design lifted a carbon-fixation pathway to 1.7 times its natural output.
entries.open: Hit rates were uneven. One task yielded a single working protein from 29 tested.

entries.title: AI-designed antibody roughly doubles grip strength in mice with a muscular dystrophy
entries.sum: Anthropic reported a preclinical antibody for LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy that went from idea to mouse data in under 18 months. One design about doubled grip strength compared with untreated mice.
entries.open: This comes from a company technical report that has not been peer reviewed. Human trials are not expected before late 2028.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false
entries.sum: The hypothesis says 3-SAT cannot be solved in sub-exponential time, and a large part of complexity theory is built on it. OpenAI says its model wrote a disproof on October 16 that was checked in Lean the next day. The paper and the formal proof are public.
entries.open: Outside experts are still working out whether the formal statement matches the claim and what the algorithm means in practice.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims a proof of local smoothing in every dimension
entries.sum: The local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation implies the Kakeya and restriction conjectures in harmonic analysis. OpenAI says its model proved it for all dimensions from two up on October 18, formalized it in Lean a day later, and published both on an expert's advice.
entries.open: Analysts have not yet confirmed the argument by hand.

entries.title: OpenAI reports a quantum chromodynamics result with a formalized Yang–Mills existence proof
entries.who: OpenAI, with a physics group led by David Gross
entries.sum: The third of three results announced together. OpenAI says the Yang–Mills existence part was formalized in Lean on October 16 and handed to a group of physicists for review.
entries.open: On November 9–10 the five-physicist group, which OpenAI chose, reported that the Lean code rebuilds cleanly and that its definitions match the standard statement of four-dimensional Yang–Mills existence, while saying it does not yet fully understand the proof. No fully independent check is on record, the 1,147-page written proof is still private, and the mass gap, the other half of the Millennium problem, is untouched. Critics including Peter Woit question whether the verified statement meets the prize problem's standard.

entries.title: OpenAI releases 722 AI-written manuscripts claiming hundreds of open problems
entries.sum: Posted to GitHub across 372 topics, the claims include a matrix multiplication exponent of 9/4, a proof of the unique games conjecture and a wide zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function. About half the manuscripts come with Lean proofs.
entries.open: Three papers were retracted and 14 revised within two days. Some formal proofs appear to establish less than the papers claim, and full review is expected to take months.

entries.title: OpenAI claims a solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem
entries.system: Multi-agent system of roughly ten thousand agents
entries.sum: The company said its system settled existence and smoothness for the fluid equations with a smooth external force, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems.
entries.open: No complete independent check has been published. A paper by Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen argues that the Lean code does not correspond to the written blow-up proof, citing at least two discrepancies; that does not by itself show the proof is wrong, and no OpenAI fix is on record. Credit is also disputed: mathematician Tristan Buckmaster says unpublished results of his reached OpenAI days earlier.

entries.title: First working viruses built from AI-generated whole genomes
entries.system: Evo 1 and Evo 2 genome language models
entries.sum: The models wrote complete bacteriophage genomes modeled on ΦX174. Of nearly 300 that were synthesized, 16 produced viable phages, and a mixture of them overcame E. coli strains that resist the natural virus.
entries.open: The hit rate was about 5% on one of the smallest genomes known. Larger genomes are still out of reach.

entries.title: OpenAI model disproves an 80-year-old conjecture on the unit distance problem
entries.sum: Using algebraic number theory, the model found ways to arrange points with more pairs exactly one unit apart than the grid-like layouts long believed to be best. Outside mathematicians checked and analyzed the argument.
